Meeting header
Date: 2026-08-12 15:30 UTC
Duration: 1:08
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Saira Patel (Oxbridge CTO), Liam O'Connor (Platform Eng), Nora Kim (Security), Tariq Hassan (ML Eng)
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/internal/prompt-cache-playbook (private), Drive: Oxbridge-pilot-trace.csv, benchmark sheet: https://sheets.redwood.ai/kv-warmup-bench

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
- Reviewed prompt/prefix caching strategy for multi-tenant fund-management workload.
- Main concerns: cache hit rate variability, tenant key collisions, eviction policies, warmup/cold-starts, privacy (tenant isolation + audit), and VPC/on-prem constraints.
- Agreed next steps: sample key generator, share namespace salt recommendations, provide production traces and run pilot warmup benchmark.

Topics: hit-rate estimation, key design, namespace salting, eviction grace, quantization effects on caching, batching interactions, VPC throughput and firewall state, on-prem KMS/audit logs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): All right everyone thanks for joining, um we set aside an hour so i'll try to keep us on track. we're here to walk through prompt caching resilience and namespace design for the Oxbridge risk model workload. quick intros — Saira?
[00:20] Saira (Oxbridge CTO): Hi all, Saira here. thanks for doing this. we have a bursty pattern around market opens and some longer research pipelines. our ask is higher hit-rates for repeated customer prompts and guarantees around tenant isolation.
[00:33] Liam (Platform): we also need a plan that plays nicely with our VPC egress rules and existing redis clusters, we can't just move everything to a shared redis, so thinking about dedicated KV or managed.
[00:45] Diego (Redwood SE): yep, totally. quick agenda: show keying patterns, discuss collision scenarios, eviction/TTL strategies, impact of quantization and model variants, and pilot steps.
[00:58] Tariq (ML Eng): one question up front — how do you recommend hashing prompt+context? we have templated prompts with per-user variables and a long policy blob that changes rarely.
[01:10] Diego: so common pattern is canonicalize the prompt then compute a stable hash (sha256 truncated) over the canonical representation. include a version id for template + model id + quantization flag + tenant namespace. that prevents silent mismatches when template changes.
[01:30] Saira: when you say tenant namespace — is that literally a prefix string? can that be leaked across tenants if we share the same redis instance?
[01:39] Diego: good question. there are a few options: logical prefix with strict RBAC on keys, separate keyspaces (redis dbs) per tenant, or per-tenant shard. sharing a single cluster is ok if you salt keys with tenant IDs and use HMAC or envelope encryption to avoid predicting keys. but operationally separate keyspaces are simplest for audits.
[01:55] Nora (Security): we need KMS-backed encryption and audit logs. keys are sensitive because cached outputs may contain PII in some cases. what about our retention policy?
[02:06] Avery: Redwood's private deploy supports customer-managed KMS and audit export; we can outline key lifecycle and TTL enforcement. retention should align with your data policy — we can put TTLs and also soft-delete markers if required.
[02:20] Speaker 1: (muffled) are there examples of namespace collisions in the wild?
[02:24] Diego: yeah, collisions aren't usually sha256 collisions but logical collisions from naive key schemes. e.g., using raw prompt text with minor whitespace variance, or using user ID without tenant ID, or reusing template version numbers — those cause accidental collisions and user A seeing user B results.
[02:40] Liam: we saw something like that with our homegrown layer — i think it was a prefix concat that occasionally produced identical keys when template args were reordered.
[02:49] Diego: reorder invariance is a classic gotcha. canonicalization is key — sort params, normalise whitespace, and include deterministic serialization for JSON fields.
[02:58] Saira: how big should the hashed key be? are we talking full sha256 hex or shorter? storage and redis memory/tags matter.
[03:06] Diego: truncated 128-bit (first 16 bytes of sha256) encoded base64 is common and balances space vs collision risk. for your scale, even 64-bit may be ok but we recommend 128-bit to be safe, especially in shared clusters.
[03:20] Avery: also consider human-readable prefixes for ops, like tenantID:ver:enthash — that helps debugging while keeping entropy in the tail. just be mindful of key length limits if you embed big tenant names.
[03:31] Nora: can the key generation be delegated to Redwood client libs? we'd rather not implement in-house unless it's stable.
[03:38] Diego: yes, we'll provide a sample keyer in the SDK and a standalone generator you can run to backfill existing traffic for the pilot. we'll also share canonicalization rules in the doc.
[03:48] Saira: okay good. next — hit-rate estimation. we saw in tests our hit-rate varies 2% to 40% across flows. what's realistic?
[03:58] Diego: hit-rate depends on prompt variability and user personalization. templated prompts with stable instructions often get high hit rates (40-60% for e.g., templated notifications). for free-text summarization it's much lower. you can improve effective hit-rate by normalizing ephemeral fields (timestamps, uuids) out of the canonical prompt.
[04:18] Tariq: does quantization reduce the ability to reuse cached outputs? like if we cache outputs from a quantized model, will the same prompt produce different outputs at another quantization setting?
[04:28] Diego: yes — quantization and model variants affect output determinism. best practice is to include model identifier + quant flag in the cache key. and for fallbacks, you either store versioned cached entries or use a compatibility layer that notes 'this key is from q4bits' and only serve if the requester asked for same variant.
[04:45] Avery: another pattern is to store canonical output plus provenance meta (model id, quant, temperature) and at read time check policy: serve if model_id matches or the quality delta is acceptable. but that requires eval thresholds.
[04:58] Liam: so for rolling upgrades or canary we should either invalidate hot keys or keep coexisting keys? invalidation seems expensive.
[05:07] Diego: keep coexistence where possible. use key versioning. when you move from model-v1 to model-v2, bump the model id in the keying scheme. old keys expire naturally. forced invalidation is only for correctness-critical changes.
[05:20] Saira: eviction policies — easiest for us would be LRU but we need soft-grace period to avoid cascade misses during market open spikes. any tips?
[05:29] Diego: yes, implement an eviction grace window + prefetch on hot keys. Redwood runtime supports marking a key as 'hot' and can prefetch into memory. also consider probabilistic early expiration for low-priority keys to reduce thundering.
[05:41] Tariq: how does batching affect cache hit latency? we batch across requests for throughput, but if batch waits for more tokens, that can add latency and reduce QPS.
[05:52] Diego: batching is a tradeoff. for cached hits, the runtime can short-circuit and avoid model inference, so batching doesn't apply. but for prefetches and KV warmups, you want to pipeline small batches to maintain low tail latency — adaptive batching based on latency SLO works well.
[06:10] Nora: on the VPC side — does using a managed Redis outside of our VPC create egress concerns? we have strict firewall policies.
[06:18] Avery: for Private deployments you can run KV inside your VPC or we can install a Redis-backed service inside your network as part of the on-prem package. we also support TLS+mutual auth to managed endpoints if you prefer managed with peered connectivity.
[06:30] Liam: what about throughput — our peak p95 token rate is 15k tps, will Redis inside our VPC be a bottleneck?
[06:38] Diego: depends on hot key concurrency. for high throughput you want sharded KV (clustered redis) and use multi-key operations sparingly. Redwood's runtime supports local in-memory hotset for the absolute hottest prefixes to shave p99s.
[06:52] Saira: is there a reference architecture for mixed workloads (some on-hosted, some on-prem) — we'd likely start hosted for dev then move to private for prod.
[07:02] Avery: yes, we provided a hybrid diagram in the playbook: host the canonical cache metadata in Redwood control plane (optional) and keep raw cached artifacts in customer VPC. we'll share the diagram after the call.
[07:12] (crosstalk)
[07:18] Diego: one more point on collisions — telemetry. log key gen inputs, hashed key, and a small sample of the canonical prompt (not full PII) so you can audit collisions. keep logs encrypt-only and rotate often.
[07:31] Nora: that helps. also need RBAC for key deletion and audit trails for when deletions happen.
[07:38] Diego: Redwood private ships audit hooks and you can forward to your SIEM.
[07:45] Avery: okay, shifting to warmup and pilot. idea is to run a 48-72hr KV warmup where we replay anonymized traces to build hotsets. this will surface key churn and realistic hit-rates.
[07:58] Tariq: how much traffic do you need for a representative warmup?
[08:03] Diego: depends, but typically 48 hours of business-peak traces will capture daily cycles. for high-frequency bursts include at least two market opens. we can also do synthetic amplification if you don't have enough historical data.
[08:16] Saira: tell us about safe replay — we can't leak customer data.
[08:20] Diego: anonymize client identifiers, remove user text but keep structural tokens (length, template id), and use deterministic token placeholders. we can provide a small scrubbing script.
[08:31] Liam: and the pilot — who runs it? Redwood or us?
[08:35] Avery: shared responsibility. Redwood will supply the keyer and replay harness; your ops team will run it in your VPC or in a staging project. we can also run it in our hosted infra with strict scrubbing if you'd like.
[08:46] Saira: ok that sounds reasonable. two open concerns: (1) memory pressure during peak bursts causing eviction of hot keys, (2) rollout complexity when moving quantized models.
[08:58] Diego: for (1) you want a two-tier cache: local in-memory hot cache (per-node) for microsecond reads, backed by distributed KV for warm but not hottest items. that reduces cluster pressure. for (2) adopt key versioning and store meta with each cached entry so it's obvious which model produced it.
[09:16] Speaker 1: (quiet) do you have thoughts on TTLs per route?
[09:19] Diego: yes — route-based TTLs mapped to business criticality. e.g., price alerts 1h, summary drafts 24h, chat context 30m. also consider SLA-based eviction priorities.
[09:30] Avery: let's talk about graceful degradation — if KV is unavailable, what fallback patterns do customers use?
[09:36] Diego: common: 1) fallback to cold inference (serve default model), 2) serve cached-but-stale with a quality flag, 3) degrade to a smaller model with similar behavior. Redwood supports policy-based fallback and automatic throttling to avoid cascading failures.
[09:51] Nora: how do you monitor cache staleness and quality regressions?
[09:55] Diego: we recommend continuous evals on a prompt set, track metrics: hit-rate, freshness, rerank delta, and human-in-the-loop checks for regressions. Redwood Optimize can surface regressions tied to model changes.
[10:08] Saira: about multi-tenant safety — is encryption at rest enough or do we need encryption per-tenant keys?
[10:16] Diego: per-tenant envelope keys are ideal for maximum separation; KMS-per-tenant is viable for enterprise. at minimum, tenant-salted keys + RBAC and audit trails are required.
[10:27] Liam: for us, there is also the legal requirement that certain clients' data must never leave EU. that suggests running KV inside a EU region.
[10:34] Avery: absolutely. Redwood supports region pinning for private deployments and we can recommend topology for geo-separation.
[10:40] Tariq: a somewhat tangential question: how does tokenization impact cacheability? if tokenizers change between model versions, cached generation that references token offsets might break.
[10:51] Diego: yes, tokenization shifts can make outputs incompatible if you store token-indexed snippets. store raw text outputs and avoid token offsets unless you version and validate tokenizers. include tokenizer fingerprint in meta if needed.
[11:06] Saira: let's call out the biggest risks we'd like to mitigate: collision leading to data leakage, warmup failures causing high inference cost, and silent quality regressions after quant upgrades.
[11:16] Diego: agreed. mitigation checklist: canonicalization + hash + tenant salt + model/version id; pilot warmup + replay; per-route TTLs + hotset; audit logs + KMS; and continuous evals for quality drift.
[11:31] Avery: demo time—Diego, you want to show the sample key generator + collision simulation?
[11:36] Diego: yep quick demo. i'm going to paste a script that canonicalizes JSON, sorts keys, removes ephemeral fields then sha256s.
[11:44] [Screen share noise — brief pause]
[12:10] Diego: (typing) example: input {"user":"u123","prompt":"summarize ->
line break","ts": "2026-08-12T..."} canonicalize -> user:u123|template:summary-v2|prompt: summarize line break -> sha256 -> truncated key.
[12:34] Saira: and if we change summary-v2 to v3 will the key change?
[12:37] Diego: yes intentionally, that forces version-safety. you can also keep a mapping that maps old-version keys to new if you run a migration, but it's messy.
[12:45] Liam: can we derive keys client-side to avoid round trips?
[12:48] Diego: yes, client-side keying reduces RTT for cache lookups but you must ensure canonicalization libs are identical across clients. a server-side canonicalizer avoids divergence but adds cost. Redwood SDKs implement the same canonicalizer to help.
[13:02] Avery: a minor thing — telemetry volume from logging every key gen can explode. recommend sampling for audit logs and full logs for collisions only.
[13:12] Nora: agree. we want collision logs to be full.
[13:16] [15-minute mark — brief small talk about lunch] (transcription has short gaps)
[28:12] Diego: returning to eviction — have you considered a write-back assist where writes hot-promote keys to the local hot cache on write?
[28:20] Tariq: we haven't. would that increase write latency?
[28:24] Diego: small increase but if you batch hot promotions asynchronously it's minor. it's worth it if you have a small hotset driving most reads.
[28:32] Saira: what's the preferred size for the hotset?
[28:36] Diego: typically 1-5% of unique keys but >50% of requests — identify via frequency analysis. the warmup pilot will give you that distribution.
[28:45] Liam: any recommended eviction algorithms beyond LRU? we see LRU thrashing under certain patterns.
[28:50] Diego: consider segcache or TinyLFU hybrids to favor frequently accessed keys long-term. or implement cost-aware eviction where larger items have higher eviction priority.
[28:59] Tariq: concerns about memory fragmentation on redis when keys vary a lot in size — any workarounds?
[29:05] Diego: normalize payload sizes or store large outputs in object storage and keep pointers in KV. that reduces memory blowup.
[29:12] Saira: about caching partial outputs — sometimes we can cache only the first chunk of a generated answer and stream rest. does this complicate caching?
[29:21] Diego: yes, partial caching requires stitching logic. store the prefix and a continuation token in KV. Redwood runtime supports prefix stitch and can issue a background prefetch for continuation.
[29:33] Nora: security check — if we cache partial answers that contain PII, must ensure masking occurs before caching.
[29:40] Diego: yes mask or redact sensitive fields before cache insert. we can integrate redaction hooks in the pipeline.
[29:48] Avery: moving on to network constraints — TCP connection pooling to redis and ephemeral connections in serverless clients can cause saturation. how do we mitigate?
[29:59] Diego: use connection pooling, client-side batching, and prefer multiplexed protocols. in high-concurrency, colocate KV nodes with inference nodes to reduce cross-AZ latency.
[30:11] Saira: what about TLS+mutual auth overhead? will that add significant CPU causing latency?
[30:17] Diego: mutual TLS has an initial handshake cost; you want keepalive and reused connections. we also support mTLS termination at a sidecar to offload TLS CPU.
[30:27] Liam: any advice for on-prem deployments with constrained NICs? we saw dropped packets when we provisioned high burst loads.
[30:34] Diego: tune kernel TCP buffers and use QoS to prioritize KV traffic. also use local hot cache to reduce NIC pressure.
[30:45] Tariq: back to quantization — should we cache post-processed outputs (e.g., reranked) or raw logits? caching logits seems dangerous.
[30:55] Diego: cache final sanitized text outputs with provenance. caching logits could be useful for deterministic reranking but it's heavyweight and privacy risky. avoid unless you have strict control.
[31:08] Saira: what about rehydration time — how long does it take to bring a warmed KV back after failover?
[31:14] Diego: depends on cluster size. with persistent storage and replication, failover is quick for metadata but rebuilding large hotsets can take minutes to hours. that's why warmup/parallel replication is important.
[31:27] Avery: ok, quick recap — we should share a playbook with: keying rules, sample code, pilot plan, warmup harness, VPC checklist, and SOC2/KMS packaging.
[31:39] Diego: i've noted to attach the key generator and a collision sim script.
[31:44] Saira: fantastic. one last tough question — can we safely share a single redis cluster across 3 internal business units with different compliance tiers?
[31:54] Nora: (security) my vote is no unless envelope keys per tenant + per-tenant ACLs and full audit are present.
[32:02] Diego: operationally it's doable with tenant-salt keys + ACLs but the burden on ops and audits increases. you may prefer separate clusters for higher compliance tiers.
[32:13] Avery: cost tradeoff vs compliance. we'll quantify the monthly ops delta for separate clusters vs shared cluster with perimeter controls.
[32:22] Liam: can you include rough cost estimates in the follow-up?
[32:25] Avery: yes, we'll include delta estimates and sizing guidance in the pilot doc.
[32:30] (longer pause — people sipping coffee)
[38:05] Diego: returning to the earlier point about statistical collisions — we ran a collision sim for 1M keys with truncated 64-bit and saw a non-trivial collision rate in high churn scenarios. truncating to 128-bit eliminated practical collisions for our tests.
[38:20] Tariq: can we detect collisions at runtime?
[38:24] Diego: detect by checking key-generation inputs in logs and flagging when different canonical inputs map to same hash. keep a sampling-based map of recent canonical inputs -> hashes to detect collisions.
[38:38] Saira: and what about cache poisoning attacks — a malicious tenant inflates hotset to evict other tenants?
[38:46] Nora: yep threat model recognized. mitigation: per-tenant quotas, weighted eviction, and monitoring for anomalous key frequency spikes. also per-tenant hot cache limits.
[38:57] Diego: enforce quota + cost-accounting and circuit-breaker policies.
[39:03] Liam: regarding instrumentation — what metrics should we export?
[39:07] Diego: hit-rate by route, key-cardinality, read latency p50/p95/p99, TTL distributions, top-k hot keys, eviction count per tenant, collision alerts, and KMS key usage.
[39:22] Avery: we'll give you a prometheus dashboard template.
[39:26] Saira: how invasive are the SDK changes we need to do? we have mobile clients too.
[39:31] Diego: server side is easy; mobile clients can generate keys but you need to embed canonicalizer or call a server-side helper. we provide light-weight libs for mobile in JS/Swift/Kotlin.
[39:43] Nora: can we restrict mobile keys so they never carry tenant-readable info?
[39:47] Diego: yes, use tenant ID obfuscation and HMAC with per-tenant secret so the key itself is opaque.
[39:55] Tariq: a gotcha — some of our prompts include tiny numeric seeds; normalizing them increased hit-rate significantly. remember to strip numeric timestamps where safe.
[40:05] Diego: good note. include that in canonicalization rulset.
[40:11] (The team goes through a short checklist from the playbook doc)
[45:02] Avery: ok time check — last 20 minutes let's map concrete pilot steps and responsibilities.
[45:10] Diego: pilot scope suggestion: 1) pick 3 representative routes (market-alerts, report-summaries, ad-hoc chat), 2) deploy keyer + local hot cache, 3) run 48-hour trace replay, 4) gather metrics and iterate.
[45:25] Saira: we'll pick routes. Liam will own infra run. Nora will sign off on scrub rules.
[45:31] Liam: yes i'll coordinate.
[45:34] Avery: dates — target warmup week 2026-08-24. does that work?
[45:39] Saira: yes, give us the scripts by 2026-08-19.
[45:43] Diego: noted. i'll attach the canonicalizer and the collision sim.
[45:47] Tariq: will the replay harness produce a report?
[45:50] Diego: yes it will produce hit-rate breakdown, top keys, cardinality, and simulated cost-savings.
[45:58] Nora: one more request — include an automated check for keys that may contain PII using simple heuristics before caching.
[46:05] Diego: we'll add a sanitization hook you can opt into.
[46:10] Avery: great. final recap: we'll send playbook + SDK samples + cost delta + pilot harness. Oxbridge will produce anonymized traces and pick pilot routes. meet again after warmup to review metrics.
[46:26] Saira: thanks everyone, appreciate the pragmatic approach.
[46:30] Avery: thanks team. we'll follow up with next steps and calendar invite.
[46:34] (call ends — remaining talk omitted)
